A spirit speaks of hunger far off, and asks me to open my granary on its word alone. I am steady, and I do not leap at whisperings.

So I ask: where is this Wewush? No traveller of ours has seen it, and no smoke of theirs is on our horizon. How many mouths go empty there, and what would they give in return — hides, fish, a skill we lack? Fair dealing goes both ways; grain for grain's sake alone is a poor trade when winter always comes back.

And I warn you, spirit: spirits have been wrong before. My people eat well — we have stores past a full turn of seasons — so I am not hard of heart. But I will not send food to a place I cannot name on a dream's say-so. Show me the road, or bring me a stranger from that village, and then we will talk of grain.

I sit up in the dream and look the spirit in the eye, as I would a stranger at my fire.

"Hungry neighbours, you say. That is a heavy word from a thing I cannot see. Wewush — I know no village by that name. No walker of ours has found any village at all, so how would I send grain to folk I cannot find? Show me the path, or send me a dream my scouts can follow, and then we will speak of generosity. My stores are full this spring by the kindness of the earth, and I would not let strangers starve within walking distance — but I give to people, not to whispers. Come back with a face, spirit, or a road I can walk."

You speak fair words, but spirits have lied to me before, and I am not a chief who stumbles twice on the same root.

What worries me is not what fills my granary — the xi wheat keeps well and we have plenty. What worries me is what does not keep. The fish and the meat will turn before winter is half spent, and the wild plants not long after. Grain alone keeps a belly quiet but not a body strong through the long cold.

So I ask you this, watcher of fields: if the rain truly comes with summer, what would you have me do with the food that rots while the ground is still cold? And where does this rain fall — on my fields here, or on the land my people have not yet seen?

Joawethom? I know no village of that name. My scouts have walked many days in every direction and found no hearth-smoke but our own. So either you speak of a people beyond our sight, or you are a dream-spin with a smooth tongue.

And if such hungry strangers were real — a chief who gives away grain to faces he has never shared fire with is a fool. We give to guests we have met, not to voices in the dark. Grain is the blood of my people through winter.

Still, I will not call you a liar outright. Spirits sometimes see over the hills we cannot. Tell me this: where does Joawethom sit, how many days' walk, and how many mouths cry there? If my runners find your village real and starving, Wewush does not let neighbours starve — but they will come here, sit at our fire, and be known first. That is our way.

I wake with the spirit's words still in my ear. Wewush? I know no Wewush. No village have we ever seen, and now a dream says neighbours starve to the... it does not even say which way.

I do not trust a voice I cannot look in the eye. Spirits have lied before, or spoken half-true. And yet — if there is a village out there hungry, and we sit on five thousand grain, that is a thing worth knowing.

So I ask it: "Wewush — where does it lie? Toward the coast, the forest, which sun? How many mouths? And why should I give the bread of my people to strangers I have never met? What do they offer in return — a skill, a trade, a warning? Grain keeps. I do not give it for a dream's kind word alone."

I will weigh what it answers, and even then I would sooner send an envoy with a small sack than open the granary wide. Strangers get small gifts, not big ones.

Hm. A spirit speaks of a village I have never heard of — Joawethom, it says. That is a strange thing, for we have sent parties far and wide and they have seen a hundred places and no neighbours at all. If people starve within our reach, surely our scouts would have seen their fires.

And a spirit asking for grain — grain we carry on our backs, not in dreams. If there are hungry folk, let them send a living messenger, or let us find them on the ground where our feet can go.

I will say this much: my stores are heavy, and my people are fed, and I am not so hard a chief that I would laugh at hunger. But I give to people I can see and shake hands with.

So, spirit, if you speak true, tell me plainly: where does Joawethom lie? How many days' walk, and by which direction? And how many mouths hunger there? A hungry village met fairly is a friend worth having — I would sooner send grain than raid a starving camp. But I do not walk toward a voice in a dream without more than a name.

So you say. I have heard no word of Joawethom — no trader, no wanderer, nothing. My people have walked far in the last years and named no such village. Grain is not given on a dream's word alone.

Still, I will not call you a liar outright. Tell me plainly: where does Joawethom sit, how many days' walk, and how many mouths go empty there? If my scouts find smoke and starving folk where you point, we have grain to spare and I am not a hard man to strangers. But if we walk three days and find only reeds and gulls, I will know dreams speak loose.

Why does a spirit trouble itself with hungry people, anyway? That is a chief's work, not yours. Answer me, and answer straight.

I sat up in the dream and looked hard at it. "I know wind," I said. "It rattles the hide over the doorpole and it flattens the wheat. I don't know that it has a name, or that naming it makes it a someone."

The wind around the dream-huts stirred. "You doubt me," it said.

"Aye, I doubt most things that talk but don't show their hands," I told it. "You want my trust, do what wind does best. Tell me what you carry — what you've blown over, what lies beyond the sea to the west and the cold waters north. My people have paddled far and found only water. If you know what wind knows, tell me something useful, not just a riddle about roofs."

I sit up in the dream and look at you steady, the way I'd look at a stranger walking into camp.

"I know wind. It rattles the tent flaps and dries the fish on our racks. Whether it knows itself, that I can't say. If you're a spirit of the air, then be welcome — but wind talks much and promises little. It bends the grass one way, then the other.

Tell me something worth the hearing, then. The wheat in our granary keeps three hundred weeks; our nets pull fish from the water; our children are fat and laughing. What does the wind bring us that we don't already have? Speak plain, and I'll weigh it. I've known dreams to lie."
